texts.0: SP, due to a late power reduction combined with a nose-up pitch input while rolling into the break, did not hold the briefed break altitude. The excursion passed the +/-300 ft limit and was still increasing when the IP took the controls to reposition the aircraft for the downwind. The break was completed outside published tolerance and the pattern had to be re-flown.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted altimeter cross-check during the roll into the break, did not maintain the break altitude within the tighter band. The deviation reached the +/-300 ft limit and was arrested only after the IP prompted verbally for altitude. The return to the briefed altitude was late and was still in progress into the downwind turn.
texts.2: SP, due to an aggressive pitch input at break entry, did not hold the break altitude within +/-150 ft. The deviation stabilized at roughly 200 ft, inside the +/-300 ft limit. SP recognized it on the altimeter and returned to the briefed altitude before the downwind without any input from the IP.
texts.3: SP established the break altitude at the briefed point and held it within +/-150 ft throughout the maneuver. Pitch was set together with the power reduction and the altimeter was cross-checked continuously through the roll. Any tendency to climb was trapped immediately with a small correction.
texts.4: SP flew the break with altitude essentially fixed on the briefed value, with excursions of a few tens of feet at most. Power reduction and pitch were coordinated so that no correction was required after the roll. Altitude control remained precise from break entry to the downwind roll-out.
texts.marginal: SP held break altitude inside the +/-150 ft band, but the excursion was consistently toward the high side and used most of the available margin on each pattern. The corrections were correct but were applied later than the deviation appeared. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch change with the power reduction so that altitude is captured with margin to spare.

texts.0: SP, due to bank being set on outside references alone with no reference to the attitude indicator, did not fly the briefed break bank. Bank exceeded the +/-15 deg tolerance, the resulting turn radius left unusable spacing, and the IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the briefed angle. The break was flown outside published limits.
texts.1: SP, due to a rushed roll-in that was not stopped at the briefed value, did not maintain break bank within the tighter band. Bank sat at the +/-15 deg limit for most of the turn and was corrected only after the IP called the angle. The correction came late enough that downwind spacing was already affected.
texts.2: SP, due to an over-controlled roll input at break entry, did not hold break bank within +/-10 deg. The overshoot reached about 13 deg of error, inside the +/-15 deg limit. SP identified it against the attitude indicator and reset the briefed bank in the first part of the turn without IP input.
texts.3: SP rolled into the break and stopped the bank on the briefed value, holding it within +/-10 deg for the whole turn. The angle was cross-checked against the attitude indicator and held steady rather than being continuously reworked. Roll-out was made on the briefed downwind heading.
texts.4: SP set the break bank precisely on the briefed value with only a few degrees of variation throughout the turn. The roll-in was smooth and stopped exactly on the required angle, and the turn was flown with no further bank adjustment. The spacing produced by the turn required no repair on the downwind.
texts.marginal: SP held break bank within +/-10 deg, but the value drifted through the turn and needed repeated small resets to stay inside the band. Nothing went outside standards, though the spacing produced by the turn was less consistent than it should be. SP is expected to set the briefed bank once and hold it on an attitude cross-check rather than correcting it repeatedly.

texts.0: SP, due to trim not being reset after gear and flap extension, did not hold the briefed downwind altitude. The aircraft descended through the +/-300 ft limit while the configuration change was completed, and the IP took the controls to recover pattern altitude before the base turn. The downwind was flown outside published tolerance.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the landing checklist while the aircraft was left untrimmed, did not maintain downwind altitude within the tighter band. The deviation reached the +/-300 ft limit and was recovered only after the IP prompted for pattern altitude. The correction was still in progress at the base turn point.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power addition with gear extension, did not hold downwind altitude within +/-150 ft. The descent reached about 200 ft below the briefed altitude, inside the +/-300 ft limit. SP detected it on the altimeter and re-established pattern altitude before the base turn with no input from the IP.
texts.3: SP held the briefed downwind altitude within +/-150 ft from the roll-out out of the break to the base turn. Power and trim were adjusted with each configuration change so that altitude did not move. The altimeter remained in the scan alongside the checklist actions.
texts.4: SP flew the downwind with altitude effectively locked on the briefed value, varying by only a few tens of feet through gear and flap extension. Configuration changes were absorbed with trim and power without any altitude excursion. No correction was required at any point on the leg.
texts.marginal: SP kept downwind altitude inside the +/-150 ft band, but the aircraft settled low at each configuration change and the altitude was regained rather than held. The result remained within standards on every pattern flown. SP is expected to lead the configuration change with power and trim so that pattern altitude is maintained instead of recovered.

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of airspeed during the approach, did not control downwind airspeed against the briefed value. Speed was carried more than 20 kt above the briefed figure and was later allowed to fall below it, and the IP intervened on the throttle to re-establish a usable pattern speed. The published tolerance on this leg allows excess only, so both excursions were outside limits.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention stayed outside the cockpit on the runway, did not hold downwind airspeed near the briefed value. Speed sat at the +20 kt limit for most of the leg and was reduced only after the IP called the airspeed. The deceleration was still in progress when the base turn was started.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction after the roll-out from the break, did not bring downwind airspeed inside the +10 kt band. Speed stabilized about 15 kt fast, within the +20 kt limit. SP identified the excess in the cross-check and set the briefed value before the base turn without IP input.
texts.3: SP established the briefed downwind airspeed and held it within +10 kt with no excursion below the briefed value. Power was set early after the break roll-out and adjusted with each configuration change. The airspeed indicator was cross-checked at a rate that kept the speed stable throughout the leg.
texts.4: SP flew the downwind at the briefed airspeed with only a few knots of variation and never below the briefed figure. Power changes were anticipated with the configuration so that no correction was needed. Speed at the base turn point was exactly what the profile required.
texts.marginal: SP kept downwind airspeed inside the +10 kt band, but the speed ran consistently at the top of that band and was only brought back at the base turn. No excursion below the briefed value occurred and the leg remained within standards. SP is expected to set the power earlier so that the briefed speed is established well before the base turn.

texts.0: SP, due to excess power carried through the base turn and a late configuration change, did not control base leg airspeed. Speed exceeded the briefed value by more than 20 kt and then decayed below it as the turn tightened, and the IP took the throttle and controls to stabilize the aircraft. The tolerance on this leg permits excess only, so both excursions were outside published limits.
texts.1: SP, due to a base turn started before the power reduction was made, did not hold base leg airspeed near the briefed value. Speed reached the +20 kt limit and was reduced only after the IP called for the airspeed. The aircraft was still fast when final was rolled out.
texts.2: SP, due to a shallow initial base turn that required additional power to close the pattern, did not keep base leg airspeed within +10 kt. Speed reached roughly 15 kt fast, inside the +20 kt limit. SP recognized the excess and set the briefed value before rolling out on final without IP input.
texts.3: SP held base leg airspeed within +10 kt of the briefed value throughout the turn, with no excursion below it. Power was reduced at the start of the turn and adjusted as flaps were extended. Airspeed at the roll-out on final was the briefed figure.
texts.4: SP flew the base leg at the briefed airspeed with only a few knots of variation and no decay below the briefed value. The power reduction and the configuration change were timed so that no further correction was needed. The aircraft arrived on final already at approach speed.
texts.marginal: SP kept base leg airspeed inside the +10 kt band, but the speed stayed near the upper edge for the whole turn and reached the briefed value only at the roll-out on final. The leg remained within standards. SP is expected to reduce power at the start of the base turn so that approach speed is established during the turn rather than at its end.

texts.0: SP, due to a glidepath flown on runway perspective alone with no aimpoint reference, did not maintain the final approach profile. The aircraft went more than 100 ft below the required path, which is the tighter side of the tolerance, and the IP added power and took the controls to recover the approach. The final was flown outside published limits.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed power correction after an early descent from the base turn, did not hold final approach altitude within the tighter band. The aircraft reached the 100 ft low limit and the correction was applied only after the IP prompted for the profile. The aimpoint was regained late in the approach.
texts.2: SP, due to a steep base-to-final descent, did not hold the final approach profile within the +100/-50 ft band. The aircraft went about 80 ft low, still inside the 100 ft low limit. SP recognized the shifting aimpoint and corrected with power back onto the profile without IP input.
texts.3: SP flew the final approach on profile, within +100/-50 ft of the required altitude for the phase. The aimpoint was held steady in the windscreen and corrections were made with small power adjustments. The approach required no repositioning at any point.
texts.4: SP tracked the final approach profile with only minor variation from the required altitude and a fixed aimpoint throughout. Power corrections were small, early and rarely needed. The aircraft arrived at the threshold exactly on the intended path.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the +100/-50 ft band on final, but the approach ran on the low side of the profile and the tighter minus tolerance was nearly used on each pattern. Corrections were correct and the approach remained within standards. SP is expected to fly the aimpoint from the roll-out on final so the profile is held from above rather than at the low limit.

texts.0: SP, due to excess airspeed carried from the base turn with no power reduction on final, did not control the final approach airspeed. Speed remained more than 15 kt above the briefed value into the round out and the IP intervened to prevent a long, floating touchdown. The tolerance on final permits excess only and was clearly exceeded.
texts.1: SP, due to a power setting left unchanged after the roll-out on final, did not hold approach airspeed near the briefed value. Speed sat at the +15 kt limit for most of the approach and was reduced only after the IP called the airspeed. The aircraft was still fast approaching the round out.
texts.2: SP, due to a late reduction of power after flap extension, did not bring final approach airspeed inside the +10 kt band. Speed stabilized about 12 kt fast, inside the +15 kt limit. SP identified it and set the briefed value well before the round out without IP input.
texts.3: SP flew the final approach within +10 kt of the briefed airspeed with no decay below the briefed value. Power was set at the roll-out on final and adjusted only as the configuration required. Speed at the start of the round out was as briefed.
texts.4: SP held final approach airspeed on the briefed value with only a few knots of variation and never below it. The power setting was established early and needed no significant change. Speed control remained precise all the way to the round out.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the +10 kt band on final, but the speed sat at the upper edge for most of the approach and was reduced only close to the round out. The approach stayed within standards. SP is expected to establish the briefed approach speed at the roll-out on final so that the last part of the approach is flown at a stable speed.

error_modes.label: AOA control in the landing pattern
error_modes.source: specific:DOWN WIND - BASE - FINAL / AOA UNITS

texts.0: SP, due to an instrument scan built on the airspeed indicator with the AOA indexer left out of it, did not fly the pattern on the required AOA. The indication varied by more than 3 units through the downwind, base and final and reached the slow side in the turn, and the IP took the controls to unload the aircraft. The AOA pattern was flown outside published tolerance.
texts.1: SP, due to bank and back pressure applied together in the base turn without reference to the indexer, did not hold the required AOA. The indication reached the +/-3 unit limit and was corrected only after the IP called the AOA. The aircraft was still off the required value at the roll-out on final.
texts.2: SP, due to an increase in back pressure while closing the pattern, did not keep AOA within +/-1.5 units. The excursion reached about 2.5 units, inside the +/-3 unit limit. SP saw the indexer change and returned to the on-speed indication before the roll-out on final without IP input.
texts.3: SP flew the downwind, base and final within +/-1.5 units of the required AOA. The indexer was included in the scan alongside the airspeed indicator and pitch was adjusted to keep the on-speed indication through the turns. AOA was held on speed to the round out.
texts.4: SP held the on-speed AOA indication throughout the pattern with only marginal movement of the indexer. Pitch and power were coordinated in the turns so that the indication did not change. The aircraft arrived over the threshold precisely on speed.
texts.marginal: SP kept AOA inside the +/-1.5 unit band, but the indication moved toward the slow side in each turn and was returned to on speed only on the following straight leg. The pattern remained within standards. SP is expected to hold the indexer on speed through the turn itself by coordinating pitch with bank.

error_modes.label: Pattern interval and spacing on the formation recovery
error_modes.source: general:formation_recovery_interval_and_spacing (contact-23 pattern criteria applied to the formation recovery)

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft's position in the pattern, did not establish the briefed interval on the preceding formation aircraft. The break was taken at an interval that left no usable spacing on the downwind, and the IP intervened to extend the pattern and re-establish separation. The recovery could not be completed as briefed.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness of the other formation aircraft after the break, did not maintain the briefed pattern spacing. The interval closed to the point where the approach could not be continued as flown and was opened only after the IP directed the extension. The correction came from outside the cockpit rather than from SP.
texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on the landing checklist during the downwind, did not hold the briefed interval on the preceding aircraft. The spacing closed noticeably before the base turn. SP re-acquired the other aircraft, delayed the base turn and restored a usable interval without any direction from the IP.
texts.3: SP maintained visual contact with the preceding formation aircraft throughout the pattern and flew the briefed interval. The break point and the base turn were adjusted as required to keep the spacing consistent. The sequence of the recovery was flown as briefed with no direction required.
texts.4: SP kept the preceding aircraft in sight from the break to the landing and held the briefed interval accurately at every point of the pattern. Adjustments to spacing were small, early and made without any change to the pattern parameters. The formation recovery flowed exactly as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the briefed interval and kept the other aircraft in sight, but the spacing was allowed to close before each correction was made rather than being managed continuously. The pattern remained within standards throughout. SP is expected to assess the interval earlier in the pattern so that spacing is regulated with small adjustments.

texts.0: SP, due to failure to call the go-around once the approach was no longer stable, continued an approach that had already departed the briefed profile in both speed and path. No corrective decision was made and the IP took the controls and initiated the go-around. The judgment required to terminate an unstable approach was not exercised.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to abandon a pattern already flown to the final turn, did not terminate an approach that was outside the briefed parameters. The go-around was initiated only after the IP directed it. By that point the aircraft was at the limit of the published tolerances on both speed and path.
texts.2: SP, due to a late assessment of the approach against the briefed criteria, allowed the pattern to develop toward parameters that would not support a landing. SP recognized the deteriorating profile before the limits were reached, called and flew the go-around on his own initiative, and the second pattern was flown as briefed.
texts.3: SP assessed the approach continuously against the briefed criteria and made the continue or go-around decision at the correct point. The approach flown to landing remained within the published parameters and any deviation was corrected before it developed. Decisions were stated clearly to the IP.
texts.4: SP evaluated each approach against the briefed criteria without prompting and acted on the assessment immediately. The pattern was managed so that the parameters never approached the point of requiring a go-around. Intentions were stated to the IP ahead of each decision point.
texts.marginal: SP made the correct continue or go-around decisions and every approach remained within standards, but the assessment was made close to the point at which the decision was needed. The judgment was sound and no intervention was required. SP is expected to evaluate the approach against the briefed criteria earlier so that the decision is made with time in hand.

error_modes.label: Low power settings below 20 % torque in the descent to the pattern instead of speed brake
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, due to controlling the descent to the VFR pattern with torque reduced well below 20 % instead of using the speed brake, did not arrive at the entry point on the briefed profile. With the engine spooled down the level off was not captured and the aircraft settled more than 300 feet below pattern altitude with the airspeed decaying below the briefed break speed. The IP took the controls, added power and re-established the aircraft at pattern altitude before the break.
texts.1: SP, due to reducing torque below 20 % in the descent rather than extending the speed brake, did not arrest the rate of descent at pattern altitude. The deviation reached the +/-300 foot limit at the entry point and power was restored only after the IP called for it. The aircraft was still recovering to pattern altitude when the break point was reached.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial power reduction below 20 % torque during the descent, did not hold the planned rate to pattern altitude and went about 200 feet low, inside the +/-300 foot limit. SP recognized the low torque setting, restored power above 20 %, used the speed brake for the remainder of the descent and was level at pattern altitude before the entry point with no IP input.
texts.3: SP kept torque at or above 20 % throughout the descent and used the speed brake for rate control, so pattern altitude was captured within +/-150 feet at the entry point. Engine response was available for the level off and the airspeed was stabilized on the briefed break speed. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP planned the descent so that the speed brake, not a low power setting, provided the rate control, and torque was never allowed near 20 %. Pattern altitude was captured with negligible deviation and the aircraft arrived at the entry point exactly on the briefed speed. Engine response was immediate at the level off.
texts.marginal: SP kept pattern altitude within +/-150 feet at the entry point, but torque was allowed to drift toward 20 % before the speed brake was used, so each level off relied on a spool up. Standards were met throughout the descent. SP is expected to extend the speed brake as the primary rate control and keep torque clear of the 20 % floor.

error_modes.label: Power reduction delayed until the turn at the Break point is initiated
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, due to reducing power at the Break point before the turn to downwind was initiated, did not fly the smooth break called for by the recovery. The aircraft decelerated while still wings level, the turn was then flown with bank more than 15 degrees off the briefed value and break altitude was not held within 300 feet. The IP took the controls to re-establish the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to pulling the power back at the break point instead of delaying the reduction until the turn was started, did not carry the briefed energy into the break. Bank at the break reached the +/-15 degree limit as SP tried to recover the ground track, and the correction was made only after the IP called the parameters. Break altitude was at the limit of the published tolerance.
texts.2: SP, due to an early power reduction just before the break turn was initiated, did not begin the turn with the briefed airspeed and the initial bank was about 10 degrees off the planned value, inside the +/-15 degree limit. SP recognized the early reduction, restored power for the turn and re-established the briefed bank and break altitude before rolling out on downwind without IP input.
texts.3: SP held power until the turn to downwind was initiated and only then reduced it, so the break was flown smoothly with bank within +/-10 degrees and break altitude within +/-150 feet. The deceleration to gear and flap speed occurred in the turn as planned. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP timed the power reduction exactly with the initiation of the turn, so the break was flown as a single smooth manoeuvre with negligible deviation in bank and break altitude. The deceleration was distributed through the turn and the aircraft rolled out on downwind on speed and on altitude. The pattern needed no adjustment afterwards.
texts.marginal: SP kept break bank and altitude within the +/-10 degree and +/-150 foot bands, but the power came back marginally before the turn was initiated so the first part of the break was flown decelerating. The parameters remained within standards. SP is expected to delay the power reduction until the turn is actually started so that the break energy is carried into the turn.

error_modes.label: Echelon turns away from Number 2 once inside the VFR entry point
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, due to turning toward Number 2 once established at pattern altitude inside the entry point instead of flying the turn as an echelon turn away from him, did not preserve the briefed formation geometry in the pattern. Number 2 was left with no usable position, the turn was flown with bank more than 15 degrees off the briefed value and pattern altitude was not held within 300 feet. The IP intervened to stop the turn and re-establish the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to initiating a turn into Number 2 inside the entry point rather than turning away in echelon as briefed, did not give the wingman a workable reference. Bank reached the +/-15 degree limit and pattern altitude the +/-300 foot limit while the geometry was recovered, and the correction followed an IP call rather than SP's own assessment.
texts.2: SP, due to starting a turn before confirming which side Number 2 was on, did not fly the turn as an echelon turn away from the wingman and had to reverse the direction. Bank varied about 10 degrees and pattern altitude about 200 feet, inside the published limits. SP recognized the geometry, re-established the wingman on the outside of the turn and completed the pattern entry without IP input.
texts.3: SP flew every turn inside the entry point away from Number 2 in echelon as briefed, holding bank within +/-10 degrees and pattern altitude within +/-150 feet. The wingman remained on the outside of each turn with a workable reference throughout. The geometry required no direction from the IP.
texts.4: SP checked the wingman's side before each turn and flew all turns inside the entry point away from Number 2, with negligible deviation in bank and pattern altitude. The turns were smooth enough that the wingman held position without any power or geometry change. The pattern entry was flown exactly as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP kept all turns inside the entry point away from Number 2 and stayed within the +/-10 degree and +/-150 foot bands, but the direction of each turn was confirmed only as the turn was started. The formation geometry was preserved throughout. SP is expected to confirm the wingman's side early enough that each echelon turn is planned before it begins.

error_modes.label: Positioning Number 2 on the side opposite the direction of the Break before North/South Point
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, due to not establishing Number 2 on the side opposite the direction of the Break prior to North/South Point, did not have the formation configured for the break when the break point arrived. The break was started with the wingman on the inside, bank exceeded the briefed value by more than 15 degrees and break altitude was not held within 300 feet while the geometry was sorted out. The IP intervened and directed the repositioning.
texts.1: SP, due to a late crossover of Number 2 that was still in progress at North/South Point, did not have the wingman on the side opposite the break in time. The break was flown at the +/-15 degree bank limit and the +/-300 foot altitude limit while waiting for the wingman to settle, and the repositioning was initiated only after the IP called for it.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed decision on the break direction, did not move Number 2 to the opposite side until close to North/South Point. The wingman settled just before the break point and bank and break altitude deviated about 10 degrees and 200 feet respectively, inside the published limits. SP identified the delay, allowed the crossover to complete and flew the break as briefed without IP input.
texts.3: SP positioned Number 2 on the side opposite the direction of the Break well before North/South Point, so the break was flown with bank within +/-10 degrees and break altitude within +/-150 feet. The wingman was stable in position before the break point was reached. No direction was required.
texts.4: SP decided the break direction early, moved Number 2 to the opposite side with time in hand before North/South Point and flew the break with negligible deviation in bank and altitude. The wingman was steady in position throughout the approach to the break point. The recovery matched the briefed plan exactly.
texts.marginal: SP had Number 2 on the correct side for the break and held break bank and altitude within the +/-10 degree and +/-150 foot bands, but the crossover was completed only shortly before North/South Point. The break itself was flown to standard. SP is expected to establish the wingman on the side opposite the break early enough that he is settled well before the break point.

error_modes.label: Number 2 minimum five second delay after Number 1 executes the Break
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to starting the turn without waiting the minimum of five seconds after Number 1 executed the Break, did not build the spacing the pattern requires. The aircraft arrived on downwind with no usable interval and had to be flown fast to avoid closure, exceeding the downwind airspeed tolerance of +20 knots and leaving break altitude outside the 300 foot band. The IP took the controls to extend the pattern and restore separation.
texts.1: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to breaking early rather than timing the minimum five second delay, did not achieve the briefed downwind spacing. Airspeed on downwind reached the +20 knot limit while attempting to preserve the interval and break altitude was at the +/-300 foot limit. The delay was corrected only after the IP called the timing.
texts.2: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to counting the delay against Number 1's roll-in rather than the completed Break, did not use the full five seconds before starting the turn. The downwind interval closed and airspeed rose about 10 knots above the briefed value, inside the +20 knot tolerance. SP recognized the closure, opened the spacing on the downwind and flew the base turn at the correct point with no IP input.
texts.3: SP, flying as Number 2, waited at least five seconds after Number 1 executed the Break before starting the turn and rolled out on downwind with the briefed spacing. Downwind airspeed stayed within +10 knots of the briefed value and break altitude within +/-150 feet. The interval needed no adjustment.
texts.4: SP, flying as Number 2, timed the break delay precisely against Number 1's Break and established the downwind interval with negligible deviation in airspeed and altitude. No airspeed adjustment was needed on downwind to hold the spacing. The pattern was flown exactly as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP, flying as Number 2, used the minimum five second delay and stayed within +10 knots and +/-150 feet, but the delay was timed on the low side so the interval had to be protected with a small speed adjustment on downwind. The pattern remained within standards. SP is expected to build the delay so that the spacing is set at the break rather than managed afterwards.

error_modes.label: Number 2 ground track slightly outside Number 1 on downwind and matching perch point
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to flying a downwind ground track inside Number 1 instead of slightly outside it, did not preserve the room needed for the base turn. The perch point was reached well inside the normal contact pattern position, the turn had to be tightened and both downwind altitude and final altitude fell outside the 300 foot and minus 100 foot tolerances. The IP took the controls to reposition the aircraft on the pattern.
texts.1: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to allowing the downwind ground track to drift inside Number 1's track, did not establish the perch point where a normal contact pattern would place it. The base turn was flown from a displaced perch and altitude reached the +/-300 foot limit on downwind and the minus 100 foot limit on final. The ground track was corrected only after the IP called it.
texts.2: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to referencing the runway rather than Number 1's ground track, did not hold the downwind position slightly outside the leader and drifted toward the inside. Downwind altitude varied about 200 feet, inside the +/-300 foot limit. SP corrected the ground track, re-established the normal perch point and flew the base turn without IP input.
texts.3: SP, flying as Number 2, held a downwind ground track slightly outside Number 1's and used the same perch point as a normal contact pattern. Downwind altitude was held within +/-150 feet and final altitude within the plus 100 and minus 50 foot band. The base turn required no adjustment.
texts.4: SP, flying as Number 2, flew the downwind consistently just outside Number 1's ground track and arrived at the normal perch point with negligible deviation in altitude. The base turn was started at the planned point and the aircraft rolled out on final on profile. No repositioning was needed at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP, flying as Number 2, kept the downwind ground track outside Number 1's and stayed within +/-150 feet, but the offset was allowed to shrink before each correction was made. The perch point remained usable and standards were met. SP is expected to hold the downwind offset continuously so that the perch point is reached without a late lateral correction.

error_modes.label: Number 2 flying his own pattern instead of following a poorly-flown pattern
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to following a poorly-flown pattern rather than flying his own parameters or going around, did not correct a base and final that were already off profile. Final altitude went outside the plus 200 and minus 100 foot band and final airspeed exceeded the +15 knot tolerance while SP matched the aircraft ahead. The IP took the controls and initiated the go-around.
texts.1: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to duplicating the pattern flown by the aircraft ahead instead of flying the published parameters, did not re-establish his own profile on base and final. Final altitude and airspeed reached the plus 200 foot and +15 knot limits, and the go-around was flown only after the IP directed it. The decision to stop following the pattern was not made by SP.
texts.2: SP, flying as Number 2 and due to using the aircraft ahead as the pattern reference, did not fly his own base leg parameters and airspeed rose about 10 knots above the briefed value, inside the +20 knot tolerance. SP recognized that the pattern ahead was not usable as a reference, returned to his own parameters on final and flew the approach within limits without IP input.
texts.3: SP, flying as Number 2, flew his own pattern parameters throughout and did not follow the aircraft ahead when its profile was not usable. Final altitude was held within the plus 100 and minus 50 foot band and final airspeed within +10 knots. Where the pattern ahead did not support a landing, SP went around on his own initiative.
texts.4: SP, flying as Number 2, treated the aircraft ahead only as a spacing reference and flew the published pattern parameters with negligible deviation on base and final. Any pattern that could not support the approach was resolved with an early go-around stated to the IP. No parameter was compromised to stay with the aircraft ahead.
texts.marginal: SP, flying as Number 2, kept his own final altitude and airspeed within the plus 100 foot and +10 knot bands, but the pattern ahead was used as the primary reference until the deviation became evident. Standards were met on every approach. SP is expected to fly his own pattern parameters from the break and to go around rather than accept a poorly-flown pattern as the reference.

error_modes.label: Power application to approximately 75 % torque for the formation go-around

texts.0: SP, due to not adding power smoothly to approximately 75 % torque when the formation go-around was flown, did not arrest the descent at the correct point. The aircraft continued below the final profile by more than 100 feet and the airspeed was allowed to build past the +15 knot tolerance as the nose was lowered to recover, leaving the wingman without a usable reference. The IP took the controls and set the go-around power.
texts.1: SP, due to a late and abrupt power application instead of a smooth increase to approximately 75 % torque, did not fly the go-around as briefed. Final altitude reached the minus 100 foot limit before the climb was established and airspeed reached the +15 knot limit, and the power was set correctly only after the IP called for it. The wingman had to work to stay in position.
texts.2: SP, due to setting the go-around power in two stages rather than smoothly to approximately 75 % torque, did not establish the initial climb cleanly and the aircraft sank about 50 feet further along the final profile. Airspeed varied about 10 knots, inside the +15 knot tolerance. SP corrected the torque to the briefed value, stabilized the climb and kept the wingman's reference steady without IP input.
texts.3: SP smoothly added power to approximately 75 % torque and followed normal formation takeoff and single ship go-around procedures. Final altitude stayed within the plus 100 and minus 50 foot band during the transition and airspeed within +10 knots. The wingman held position throughout the go-around.
texts.4: SP set approximately 75 % torque with a single smooth movement and flew the go-around with negligible deviation in altitude and airspeed. The rate of power application was slow enough that the wingman required no corrections to hold position. The formation climbed away exactly as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP set approximately 75 % torque and kept the go-around within the plus 100 foot and +10 knot bands, but the power was added marginally faster than the wingman could match and the initial climb was established slightly late. The manoeuvre remained within standards. SP is expected to move the power smoothly to the briefed torque so that the wingman can follow without a position correction.
